solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

definitions.meaning: a verb: to put an end to, as a rumour is quashed

explanation.surface: Someone suggests pausing a journey to have a drink.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark invites a pub stop, but 'stop' is a verb here: to scotch something is to quash it.
explanation.definitionFit: Two senses: a verb meaning to put an end to, as a rumour is quashed, and the whisky distilled in Scotland.

clue.text: General shot right for photographic device

indicators.note: shot as in wrecked or ruined, so the letters of GENERAL are knocked into a new order

parts.note: anagram fodder
R = right, the standard abbreviation, added to the mix

explanation.surface: A general is photographed, or shot, from the right-hand side.
explanation.walkthrough: 'General shot' paints a military figure gunned down or photographed; 'General' is just letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by function: the darkroom machine projects a negative onto paper to make a bigger print.

clue.text: Go early and take legs over arm?

definitions.meaning: to act too soon, like a sprinter leaving before the starting pistol
literally leap (take your legs) over a firearm (an arm)

explanation.surface: A gymnast is told to start early and vault legs over an arm.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Arm' reads as a limb, but it is a weapon, a gun; the question mark flags that the second half is a literal, whimsical reading of the phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom from athletics, leaving before the starting pistol, so acting prematurely; the second reading takes the phrase literally.

parts.note: to win something is to obtain it
E = energy, as in E = mc²

explanation.surface: Someone is told to get an energy drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Energy drink' reads as one sporty product, but the two words split: energy gives E and drink is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by category: fermented grape juice is one kind of drink.

indicators.note: drunk as in staggering and muddled, so the letters lurch into a new order

parts.note: anagram fodder, 10 letters

explanation.surface: Advice not to save a drunk who must fend for himself.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drunk' looks like the person who needs rescuing, a noun; it is the instruction to jumble the letters before it.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: with no companion or chaperone means on your own.

definitions.note: Amen is an interjection affirming what is said; 'without a doubt' is used the same way, as an emphatic 'truly'.

parts.note: taken as it stands
a crew is a team of men

explanation.surface: A crew described as certain, beyond question.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Amen to that' is said to agree emphatically, which is why an exclamation of certainty can define it.
explanation.definitionFit: A liturgical word meaning 'truly' or 'so be it', used in speech as emphatic agreement, just as 'without a doubt!' is.

parts.note: under someone's influence is to be in their power
a sect is the kind of group ruled by a Svengali, a manipulative leader

explanation.surface: A sycophant is under the spell of a manipulative mentor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Crawler' suggests a toady, which fits the surface; it is a creepy-crawly. Svengali, the hypnotist in du Maurier's novel Trilby, stands for anyone controlling followers, as a cult leader controls a sect.
explanation.definitionFit: Informal sense: bugs and beetles are creepy-crawlies, so a crawler is a fair name for one.

clue.text: All The King's Men (in black and white?)

definitions.text: All The King's Men (in black and white?)

parts.note: the pieces that serve the king on a chessboard
the two colours of the pieces

explanation.surface: The title of a book or film, perhaps a black-and-white one.
explanation.walkthrough: All the King's Men is a novel and a film, and 'black and white' suggests old cinema; the king's men are really chess pieces, all of which together make a set.
explanation.definitionFit: The whole clue describes the pieces, king's men in two colours, and all of them together make up the set.

parts.note: Con = Conservative, the British political party
a fusion is a merger

explanation.surface: A merger of political parties ends in chaos.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' looks like a container instruction but only joins the definition to the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: disorder and bewilderment are what chaos amounts to.

parts.note: much = lots; these are the outer letters
n is the algebraic symbol for an unknown number; it goes inside

explanation.surface: Someone eats a great deal, the quantity never measured.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Eat lots' reads as one instruction, but only 'Eat' is the definition; 'lots' is MUCH.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym with a manner attached: chewing steadily and audibly is a way to eat.

clue.text: March, time on vacation: Apr is, unfortunately, coming in

indicators.note: things going badly, so the letters of APR IS fall out of order
the rearranged letters come into the emptied TIME
vacated, emptied, so TIME loses its middle and leaves T…E

parts.note: TIME emptied of its middle: the outer letters T and E
APRIS rearranged; it goes between T and E

explanation.surface: A diary entry: March, then holiday time, but April sadly arrives.
explanation.walkthrough: 'March' and 'Apr' plant the calendar, but March is a verb, to walk wearily; APR is just letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to walk wearily or trudge somewhere is to march, reluctantly.

clue.text: Last of horses, except for grey

parts.note: last letter of horseS
unless = except if, except for

explanation.surface: The last horses left, apart from the grey one.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Grey' looks like a horse's colour, finishing the picture; it describes a dull, overcast day.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by description: an overcast day with no sunshine looks grey.

indicators.note: in the end, so the final letter of each word is taken

parts.note: the last letters of witH nO cracklinG

explanation.surface: A pig roast that has ended up without any crackling.
explanation.walkthrough: Crackling is the crisp roasted pork skin, which suits a pig; here the words matter only for their last letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the word is used especially of a castrated male pig reared for meat.

indicators.note: to doctor is to tamper with, so the letters are altered

parts.note: anagram fodder, 11 letters

explanation.surface: An old physician praises doctors for their foresight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Doctors' sits right beside 'medic' and looks like a plural noun; it is a verb meaning tampers with.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by description: the Greek physician of the 5th century BC, father of medicine and namesake of the doctors' oath.

parts.note: to pepper is to riddle, as with shot
in mint condition = perfect

explanation.surface: A puzzle about the ideal tangy taste.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Riddle' reads as a puzzle, a noun; it is the verb, to pierce all over, as bullets pepper a target.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the mint oil used in sweets and toothpaste gives a sharp, cool taste.

clue.text: Working out like that, learner in new routine

indicators.note: made new, so the letters of ROUTINE take a fresh order

parts.note: ROUTINE rearranged; these are the outer letters, split RE…UTION
so = like that, as in 'do it so'
L = learner, from the L-plate on a learner driver's car

explanation.surface: A gym-goer's new exercise routine, learned just so.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is all gym talk; 'Working out' is really the solving of a problem, and the whole word also nods at a New Year's resolution to exercise.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the problem-solving sense: finding the answer is working it out.

clue.text: Opening of sweeties for good kid

parts.note: first letter of Sweeties
pro = for, in favour of
G = good, the standard abbreviation

explanation.surface: Opening a bag of sweets as a reward for a well-behaved child.
explanation.walkthrough: 'For' looks like a link word joining the pieces; it is PRO. Sprog is British slang for a child.
explanation.definitionFit: A regional use: British slang for a child.

clue.text: How teams played, up to a point

indicators.note: played about with, so the letters move into a new order

parts.note: anagram fodder, 8 letters

explanation.surface: A match report on how the teams played until one scored a point.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Up to a point' sounds like a scoreline; it means partly, to some extent.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to some extent, partly, is the idiom 'up to a point'.

indicators.note: rejected, thrown back, so the word is turned round

parts.note: top = first, as in top of the class; this gets turned round

explanation.surface: Someone turns down the first prize.
explanation.walkthrough: 'First prize' reads as one phrase; split it, and 'prize' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a trophy cup, or the pot of money in a card game, is a prize.

indicators.note: what the ears take in is the sound of the word, not its spelling

parts.note: sent = launched, dispatched; say it and you hear the answer

explanation.surface: A new perfume is launched, pitched at the listener.
explanation.walkthrough: Perfume is for the nose, so 'for one's ears' jars on purpose: it tells you to hear the answer rather than smell it.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a fragrance worn on the skin is a perfume.

definitions.meaning: figuratively thrilling, like a charged atmosphere
the amplified kind, as opposed to acoustic

explanation.surface: A thrilling performance by guitar players.
explanation.walkthrough: The dash and the question mark mark the second half as a description, completing the phrase 'electric guitar'.
explanation.definitionFit: Two senses: figuratively thrilling, as a charged atmosphere is, and literally amplified by electricity, as an instrument can be.

indicators.note: roaming off course, so the letters stray into a new order

parts.note: anagram fodder, 11 letters

explanation.surface: The perfect moment to look at a wandering star, a planet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wandering star' is a planet, the literal Greek meaning, and pulls the eye skywards; the star is a film actor.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: a handsome actor adored by fans, named for afternoon performances, is a star.

clue.text: Sample first of steaming potato jackets

parts.note: tater, informal for potato; these are the outer letters
first letter of Steaming; it goes inside

explanation.surface: Trying a steaming-hot jacket potato.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jackets' reads as the potato skins, a noun; it is a verb, wraps, placing TATER round the S. A jacket potato is a baked potato in its skin.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a small portion offered to try is a sample.

indicators.note: swallowed by, so the answer is inside the following words

parts.note: inside scoundrEL Firewater

explanation.surface: A villain gulps down strong liquor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spirit' and 'firewater' both suggest hard liquor, which is the trap: the spirit is a supernatural sprite.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the little folklore creature is one kind of spirit.

parts.note: to forge is to engineer, bring about; these are the outer letters
taken as it stands; it goes inside

explanation.surface: An engineer sketching the plan for a search.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Engineer' looks like a person; it is a verb, to forge or contrive.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: rummaging about, especially for food, is searching.

clue.text: Clobber dressing fashionable set, outfit in claret and blue

indicators.note: fashioned into a new shape, so SET is rearranged

parts.note: to clobber is to hit hard, wham; these are the outer letters
SET rearranged; it goes after the W

explanation.surface: Fashion talk: clothes (clobber) dressing a stylish set in a claret-and-blue outfit.
explanation.walkthrough: Clobber is British slang for clothes, which suits the fashion surface, but here it is the verb, to hit. West Ham United is a London football club that plays in claret and blue.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by description: the London football club plays in claret and blue, and 'outfit' means a team.

clue.text: Disguise alter ego on the phone?

indicators.note: heard down a phone line, so it is the sound that counts

parts.note: Mr Hyde is Dr Jekyll's alter ego in Stevenson's story

explanation.surface: Someone masks their other self when on a call.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Disguise' and 'alter ego' both suggest a secret identity; the alter ego is the specific one, Mr Hyde.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: concealing something is a way of disguising it.

clue.text: Turner has to put in something black after gold brushed over

parts.note: or is gold in heraldry; turned round it comes first
tar is black; these are the outer letters
taken as it stands; it goes inside

explanation.surface: The painter J M W Turner adds a dab of black after the gold is brushed over.
explanation.walkthrough: The Turner is a thing that turns, not the painter; 'after' puts TATOR behind the reversed gold.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by function: anything that spins or rotates something is a turner.

indicators.note: a piece taken from the words that follow

parts.note: inside ephemeRA REmarkably

explanation.surface: A collector remarks on an unusual piece of ephemera.
explanation.walkthrough: Ephemera are collectable throwaway items like tickets, which suits 'rare' in a dealer's sense.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: seldom found means unusual.

definitions.meaning: per person, as tickets are priced per diner; two words in this sense

explanation.surface: Everyone is in the lead.
explanation.walkthrough: The enumeration (5) hides that the first sense is two words, A HEAD, meaning per person.
explanation.definitionFit: Two senses: A HEAD, as in 'ten pounds a head', means per person; and in the lead means winning.

clue.text: Moving swiftly past supposition, finally getting to the point

parts.note: last letter of suppositioN
arrowing = shooting along like an arrow

explanation.surface: A speaker skips past an assumption to reach the main point.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Getting to the point' sounds like cutting to the chase in talk; it describes tapering to a tip.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by description: tapering to a tip is literally getting to a point.
